talentsSkipWildcards.Name: Talents skip wildcard skills
talentsSkipWildcards.Hint: A Talent adds nothing to a wildcard skill, even one covering the skills on its list (Monster Hunters 1 p. 24).

holyAttacks.Name: Holy attacks
holyAttacks.Hint: Contact with holy water or a holy weapon burns a creature with a Weakness to holy things for 1d, ignoring DR, then fizzes for a minute in which no holy source hurts it again (Monster Hunters 1 p. 51).

ritualPathMagic.Name: Ritual Path Magic
ritualPathMagic.Hint: Magic as nine IQ/Very Hard Path skills, each held to the lower of Thaumatology and 12 + Magery and defaulting to Thaumatology-6 (no higher than 12), with a mana reserve of Magery x 3. Magery no longer adds to Thaumatology (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 24, 32-39).

monsterHuntersGear.Name: Monster Hunters gear
monsterHuntersGear.Hint: Gadgets and clothing take improvements priced by cost factor (cutting-edge, disguised, rugged, good and fine quality, scent-masking, undercover), and Signature Gear costs a point per $10,000 of each item (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 53-54, 59).

bonusPointSpending.Name: Destiny and wildcard points
bonusPointSpending.Hint: Destiny points and wildcard bonus points join unspent points in buying successes, flesh wounds and player guidance; the GM starts each session to refresh them (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 23, 28, 31).

MH1.TalentSkipsWildcard: Talents never add to wildcard skills (Monster Hunters 1 p. 24)
MH1.DestinyHint: Spent as bonus character points; one regained each session, never more than you started with (Monster Hunters 1 p. 23).
MH1.WildcardHint: One bonus point per 12 points in the wildcard skill, handed out each session; they don't accumulate, and pay only for that skill's rolls (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 28, 31).
MH1.GmDestinyHint: A negative Destiny: the GM sets these aside each session to spend against you (Monster Hunters 1 p. 23).
MH1.FullyTrainedHint: 12+ points in a wildcard skill: ignore penalties for familiarity, exotic equipment and tech level differences, but not improvised or low-quality gear (Monster Hunters 1 p. 28).
MH1.NewSessionHint: Hand out wildcard bonus points, regain a destiny point, and set aside the GM's destiny points (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 23, 28).
MH1.WildcardOnlyItsSkill: Wildcard bonus points pay only for that skill's rolls.
MH1.NotEnough: Not enough points in that pool.

Holy.Title: Holy attack
Holy.Burns: {name} is burned by {source}: {injury} injury, ignoring DR ({from} → {to} HP). It fizzes for a minute.
Holy.Fizzing: {name} is still fizzing from the last burn: {source} does nothing for another {seconds} s.
Holy.Rule: 1d ignoring DR, then a minute in which no holy source does more (Monster Hunters 1 p. 51).
Holy.ContactHint: Touch whoever is targeted with this: a creature with a Weakness to holy things takes 1d, ignoring DR, unless it is still fizzing (Monster Hunters 1 p. 51).
Holy.NoTarget: Target who is being touched with it first.
Holy.NoEffect: Nobody targeted is hurt by holy things, or all of them are still fizzing.
Holy.CannotApply: You can't change {name}: ask the GM to apply the holy contact.

Ritual.MasteryHint: +2 to all Path skill rolls for this ritual (Monster Hunters 1 p. 25).
Ritual.MasteryChangedHint: The definition has changed since it was mastered: it counts as a different ritual (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39).
Ritual.RecordMasteryHint: Record this definition as the one Ritual Mastery is for.
Ritual.BlockingHint: The GM agrees this ritual makes sense as an out-of-turn defense: it is offered on attacks as a blocking spell (Monster Hunters 1 p. 37).
Ritual.Title: Rituals
Ritual.Hint: Written down once, with what each costs and the Path it is rolled against (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 33-35).
Ritual.CostHint: (Spell effects + modifiers) x Greater effects multiplier, less any traditional trappings (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 33-34).
Ritual.PathPenaltyHint: -1 to every roll for each Path past the second (Monster Hunters 1 p. 35).
Ritual.DurationConflictHint: Damage and healing cannot be combined with a duration (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).
Ritual.NoEffects: No effects yet: a ritual needs at least one.
Ritual.DefinitionHint: What makes this ritual this one: change any of it and Ritual Mastery or a grimoire no longer applies (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39).
Ritual.AfflictionPercentHint: +1 energy for every +5% the affliction is worth as an enhancement to Affliction; stunning costs nothing (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).

DamageKind.label: Damage priced as
DamageKind.heavy: Corrosion, fatigue, huge piercing or impaling (x2)

Ritual.TraitsAddedHint: +1 energy per character point of advantages or attributes added, or disadvantages reduced (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).
Ritual.TraitsRemovedHint: +1 energy per 5 character points of disadvantages added, or attributes or advantages reduced (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).
Ritual.MetaMagicHint: Dispelling or altering magic costs the energy of the original spell (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).
Ritual.YearsHint: For durations over a year, the added energy is the number of years + 21 (Monster Hunters 1 p. 35).
Ritual.SubjectWeightHint: For a physical change, the weight of the largest single subject, not of them all (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).
Ritual.TrappingsHint: The GM's discount of up to 25% for cool, flavourful embellishments (Monster Hunters 1 p. 34).

RitualPath.Title: Ritual Path Magic
RitualPath.CeilingHint: No Path skill may exceed the lower of Thaumatology and 12 + Magery (Monster Hunters 1 p. 32).
RitualPath.AdeptHint: Gathers in seconds rather than minutes, with none of the non-adept penalties (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 25, 36).
RitualPath.NonAdeptHint: Gathering takes minutes, and connection, consecrated space and lacking Magery each cost -5 (Monster Hunters 1 p. 36).
RitualPath.ReserveHint: Magery x 3 points of energy, drawn on in a second; refilled with Path of Magic, and assumed full after downtime (Monster Hunters 1 p. 36).

RitualCast.ExtendTooLong: An extension cannot lengthen a ritual by more than its original duration.
RitualCast.Stacking: Shares {effects} with {other}: on the same subject, only {survivor} remains (the one that took more energy).
RitualCast.Defused: {name} is defused without effect: no more than {limit} conditional rituals can hang at once.
RitualCast.Hanging: Hanging until its condition is met ({count} of {limit}).
RitualCast.Triggered: {source}: it goes off with its original margin of {margin}.
RitualCast.TriggerWaiting: {name}'s player or the GM starts it on their sheet.
RitualCast.NotYours: {name}'s mana reserve is not yours to draw on: their player or the GM can.
RitualCast.RefillNotYours: {name}'s mana reserve refills to {max}, for their player or the GM to top off.
RitualCast.CannotCancelConditional: A conditional ritual cannot be cancelled by its caster; the GM can remove it.
RitualCast.Conditional: Cast conditionally (it hangs until the condition is met)
RitualCast.ConditionPlaceholder: The condition, e.g. anyone but us enters the room
RitualCast.BreakHint: A Ready maneuver: the object breaks and its ritual goes off with its original margin (Monster Hunters 1 p. 38).
RitualCast.BreakConfirm: Break {item}? It is destroyed and its ritual goes off.
RitualCast.UseGrimoireHint: Read from the grimoire: its bonus to every roll, and all casting times doubled (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39).
RitualCast.JoinHint: Target the characters working this ritual together. Each adds their energy, and every roll is at -1 per caster past the first (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39).
RitualCast.CannotJoin: {name} cannot work this ritual: no Path within reach.
RitualCast.Blocked: Blocked: the ritual works in time, and counts as the active defense.
RitualCast.BlockFailed: The ritual isn't quick enough to work.
RitualCast.BlockingNote: A blocking ritual, at most once per turn: instant gathering at -10, tapping at -5. A caster who fails gets no other active defense unless using All-Out Defense (Double Defense) (Monster Hunters 1 p. 37).
RitualCast.Connected: Connected to the subject (present, located, or something of theirs)
RitualCast.AdeptTimes: Working at an adept's speed (-5, and tapping needs a roll)
RitualCast.DesecratedHint: Desecrated ground produces no ambient energy; only sources can be tapped.
RitualCast.GatheredQuick: gathered {energy}, and the next attempt takes one second
RitualCast.GatheredQuirk: gathered {energy}, and the spell picks up a quirk
RitualCast.Backfire: the ritual fails horribly. The GM turns {energy} energy against the caster and friends.
RitualCast.TapFailed: the source could not be tapped
RitualCast.Abandoned: Abandoned with {energy} energy gathered; it is released harmlessly.
RitualCast.Retry: the energy doesn't flow. Concentrate {seconds} more seconds, then try again.
RitualCast.Cast: the ritual works, by a margin of {margin}
RitualCast.InformationRolled: The GM rolled the final roll in secret.
RitualCast.InformationRolledRetry: The GM rolled in secret: the energy did not flow. Try again.
RitualCast.InformationRetry: a failure: the caster must try again
RitualCast.InformationLie: failed by 5 or more: the GM lies
RitualCast.ReservePrompt: Energy to draw ({reserve} in the reserve)
RitualCast.NoDonors: Everyone here has already given to this ritual.
RitualCast.NoEffects: This ritual has no effects to cast.
RitualCast.Uncastable: {path} is out of reach: this ritual cannot be worked.
RitualCast.CannotApply: You do not have permission to change: {names}
RitualCast.MageryOffThaumatology: Magery doesn't add to Thaumatology under Ritual Path Magic (Monster Hunters 1 p. 24)
RitualCast.PathCapped: Held to the lower of Thaumatology and 12 + Magery (Monster Hunters 1 p. 33)
RitualCast.PathDefault: Thaumatology-6, no higher than 12 (Monster Hunters 1 p. 33)
RitualCast.SwitchOff: Ritual Path Magic is switched off in the Rules settings.
RitualCast.NotYourCard: Only the GM, or the player who started this casting, can move it on.

Grimoire.Title: Grimoire
Grimoire.Hint: Add the rituals this book teaches to make it a grimoire (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39).
Grimoire.ChangedHint: The ritual's definition has changed since it was chosen, so this book no longer teaches it (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39). Choose it again to rebind.
Grimoire.DeadLanguageHint: Full bonus for Native comprehension, -1 for Accented, half for Broken, none without it or a translation (Monster Hunters 1 p. 39).
Grimoire.Price: As a new book: ${cost}, {weight} lbs. (Monster Hunters 1 p. 57)

Gadget.Title: Improvements
Gadget.CuttingEdgeHint: The latest materials: weight x2/3, +1 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 54).
Gadget.DisguisedHint: Resembles something else of a similar shape; finding it out takes a Search roll, or Observation in plain sight. +4 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 54).
Gadget.RuggedHint: Shockproof and waterproof: +2 on rolls to avoid breakage and water damage, weight x1.2, +1 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 54).
Gadget.ScentMaskingHint: -4 to Smell rolls to find or track the wearer. +2 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 59).
Gadget.UndercoverHint: Helps conceal weapons: +1 Holdout for +4 CF, +2 for +19 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 59).
Gadget.HoldoutHint: The Holdout bonus the article gives of itself; Undercover adds to it.
Gadget.Priced: Cost factor +{cf}, weight x{weight}, from a list price of ${cost} and {listWeight} lbs. Good and fine quality add +4 and +19 CF, except on tool kits and labs.
Gadget.SignatureHint: Each item marked as Signature Gear costs 1 point for every $10,000 or fraction of its price (Monster Hunters 1 p. 53).
Gadget.SmellNote: {penalty} to Smell rolls to find them
Gadget.ListCostHint: The table's price before improvements; left at 0, the item's own price is the list price (Monster Hunters 1 p. 54).
Gadget.ListWeightHint: The table's weight before improvements; left at 0, the item's own weight is the list weight.

WeaponImprovement.BalancedHint: +1 to skill with the weapon. +4 CF; not for sticks (Monster Hunters 1 p. 59).
WeaponImprovement.TitaniumHint: Weight x3/4 and -2 to odds of breakage, not cumulative with fine or very fine. +1 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
WeaponImprovement.WeightedHint: +1 damage. Two-handed axes and maces only: +1 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
WeaponImprovement.CompoundHint: ST+2 for damage and range. +1 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
WeaponImprovement.ImprovisedHint: An improvised weapon's skill penalty, e.g. -1 for a pool cue; Improvised Weapons for the skill removes it (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 25, 60).
WeaponImprovement.Priced: Cost factor +{cf} from a list price of ${cost} and {weight} lbs. Fine is free; very fine +3 CF (swords and fencing weapons); silver +19; silver-coated +2; holy +4, at least $250 (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 59-61).

Problem.veryFineNotSword: Very fine is for swords and fencing weapons only (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
Problem.silverCombination: Silver cannot be combined with fine, very fine or titanium (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
Problem.weightedNotTwoHandedAxe: Weighted is for two-handed axes and maces only (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
Problem.compoundNotBow: Compound is for bows and crossbows only (Monster Hunters 1 p. 60).
Problem.cheapNotOffered: Monster Hunters gear has no cheap grade; the weapon is priced as good (Monster Hunters 1 p. 59).

SpecialAmmo.PowderHint: One powder option per load (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
SpecialAmmo.PayloadHint: One payload option per load. Shotgun payloads fire as slugs, except silver (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
SpecialAmmo.MagazineHint: An empty magazine or speedloader's price. Special ammunition's CF multiplies the rounds, not this (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
SpecialAmmo.HandLoadHint: An Armoury (Small Arms) roll per asterisked option, with a reloading press: success -2 CF, failure +2 CF (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
SpecialAmmo.HandLoadGood: {option}: rolled {roll} vs {level}, a good batch (-2 CF)
SpecialAmmo.FollowUpHint: The load's follow-up attack; roll it after the bullet (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).

Problem.shotgunOnly: That payload is for shotguns only (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
Problem.notShotgun: That payload is for pistols, rifles and SMGs, not shotguns (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
Problem.dragonsBreathPowder: Dragon's Breath cannot be combined with any powder option (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).

NoteHint.silent: Greatly reduces the odds of being heard: -5 to Hearing Shots (Monster Hunters 1 pp. 61, 63).
NoteHint.smoke: Releases smoke in a 4-yard radius for 20 seconds on impact (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63; Campaigns p. 439).
NoteHint.tearGas: Releases tear gas in a 4-yard radius for 20 seconds on impact (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63; Campaigns p. 439).
NoteHint.dragonsBreath: A cone 75 yards long and 10 yards wide at the end. The gun cannot fire again for three seconds (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
NoteHint.explosive: If the slug penetrates DR, the follow-up damage is tripled and ignores DR. +1 to Hearing Shots (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
NoteHint.flare: Shot into the air, it lights a 50-yard radius for 20 seconds; darkness there is no worse than -3 (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
NoteHint.rockSalt: No damage. Living things and zombies roll HT+DR or suffer moderate pain for minutes equal to the margin of failure; salt ignores zombies' High Pain Threshold. A failed roll after a shot to the face destroys a zombie (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
NoteHint.silver: Solid silver: wounds what silver wounds (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).
NoteHint.wooden: A shot to the heart counts as a stake for vampires (Monster Hunters 1 p. 63).

powerstones.Name: Powerstones
powerstones.Hint: A stone's capacity prices it, it recharges by the mana where it is, and a carried stone can pay for a spell in place of fatigue: a One-College stone for its college, a dedicated or exclusive one for its item's spells.

spellAttacks.Name: Jets, breaths and rains
spellAttacks.Hint: A Regular spell whose record declares an attack rolls it as it is cast and each turn it lasts, dodged or blocked but not parried; an Area spell's damage falls each second on everyone in the area, halved for less than a whole second.

Powerstone.Title: Powerstones
Powerstone.IsStoneHint: An object holding mana a wizard can spend in place of his own energy
Powerstone.SetIntoHint: The magic item whose spells this stone pays for, by name
Powerstone.PricedHint: An ordinary stone's price follows its capacity, by the table in Magic
Powerstone.RechargeHint: Adds what the mana here gives back for the world time passed since the last recharge. Of the stones a character carries, only the largest recharge.

SpellAttack.AttackHint: This turn's attack: rolled against the spell's Innate Attack skill, dodged or blocked but not parried
SpellAttack.RainHint: Rolls the spell's damage for the creatures in the area to take through the damage card, with armor protecting as usual. No attack roll and no defense.
SpellAttack.RainPartial: Less than a whole second in the area (half)
SpellAttack.NoDamage: {spell} does what its description says; roll it by hand

committedDefensiveAttack.Name: Committed and Defensive Attack
committedDefensiveAttack.Hint: Two maneuvers between Attack and the All-Out ones. Committed Attack: +2 to hit or +1 damage, a second step at -2, and defenses at -2 with no retreat. Defensive Attack: -2 damage, or -1 per die, for +1 to a defense or an unbalanced weapon that can still parry.

allOutAttackOptions.Name: All-Out Attack (Long) and slams
allOutAttackOptions.Hint: All-Out Attack (Long): a yard more reach, swings at -2 damage or -1 per die, and a DX roll to end in a crouch. A slam, flying tackle, pounce or shield rush may take All-Out Attack at full Move with Determined, Feint or Strong.

moveAndAttack.Name: Move and Attack with any melee attack
moveAndAttack.Hint: Move and Attack allows a parry with what didn't strike. There is no retreat, no dodge after a kick or bite, no block with a shield that struck, and no Rapid Strike or Deceptive Attack, and a thrust may use slam damage where that is better.

acrobatics.Name: Acrobatics in combat
acrobatics.Hint: Acrobatic Stand from the ground; movement stunts (banister sliding, skidding, spinning, swinging, tic-tacs, tumbling, vaulting) that make the next dodge +2 or -2; and Acrobatic and Flying Attacks as Move and Attack.

postures.Name: Postures, hit locations and techniques
postures.Hint: Each posture's hit location effects, prohibited attacks and modified attacks, on top of the usual posture and location modifiers; and dropping to kneeling, crawling, prone, sitting or face-up as part of an attack.

feints.Name: Beats, Ruses and defensive feints
feints.Hint: A feint may be made as a Beat against one defense or a Ruse on IQ, or turned on the foe's next attack. Anyone resists with their best combat skill or a Feint technique, and Evaluate offsets feints and Deceptive Attacks from the evaluated foe.

readying.Name: Readying weapons
readying.Hint: Multiple Fast-Draw at -2 per earlier draw with the hand, Fast-Draw from odd positions and carry locations, a Ready that combines drawing with a grip change, rapid grip changes, and quick-readying a weapon from the floor, a rack or the ground.

meleeOptions.Name: Grips, Pummeling, Tip Slash and Telegraphic Attack
meleeOptions.Hint: Defensive Grip and half-swording, Reversed Grip with its forearm parry, Pummeling and Tip Slash as attack modes, and Telegraphic Attack. A weapon's grip is set by a Ready in the Readying section.

styles.Name: Styles and Style Familiarity
styles.Hint: Whether a character knows each style they have Style Familiarity for, and their Style Perk allowance, on the Skills tab (warnings only). Style Familiarity with every style a foe knows takes 1 off his feints and Deceptive Attacks.

training.Name: Training equipment and The Training Sequence
training.Hint: A character's training equipment adds to Teaching rolls, and a GM tool runs The Training Sequence for a master and students.

weaponBuilding.Name: Weapon balance, custom quality, combination and hidden weapons
weaponBuilding.Hint: Balance and custom quality levels, combination-weapon accessories with their attack modes, and concealment (rigs, trick weapons, special clothing, disguises) on a weapon's item sheet, priced in the book's order. Holdout and trick-weapon buttons on the weapon's row.

finerHitLocations.Name: New hit locations
finerHitLocations.Hint: Ear, jaw, joints, nose, spine, and veins and arteries as called shots, the skull and face from behind, crushing blows at the vitals, the 1d sub-rolls on random hits, and the lasting results of an ear, nose, spine or joint wound for the GM to confirm.

multipleAttacks.Name: Multiple attacks
multipleAttacks.Hint: Attacks from the maneuver and Extra Attack (All-Out Attack (Double) adds one), a Rapid Strike option applied to every attack in it, one special option per maneuver, a target picked per attack with an attack used up per yard skipped, feints traded for attacks, and no grappling move repeated on the same foe in a turn.

cinematicRapidStrike.Name: Cinematic Rapid Strike
cinematicRapidStrike.Hint: A Rapid Strike may have more than two attacks, at -6 per attack past the first on each (halved with Trained by a Master or Weapon Master). The GM may reserve it for those advantages, or cap adjusted skill at 12.

defenseOptions.Name: Active defense options
defenseOptions.Hint: Cross Parry and Supported Parry, Dive, Sideslip and Slip, Riposte, leg parries, a long two-handed weapon's parry against both halves of a Dual-Weapon Attack, and the fencing and two-handed refinements to multiple parries.

limitedDefenses.Name: Limits on dodging and blocking
limitedDefenses.Hint: -1 per dodge after the first in a turn, more than one block at -5 each (less for a Weapon Master), and dodging firearms only with evasive movement against the shooter. Trained by a Master and Weapon Master fighters are exempt from the dodge limits, as the book recommends.

targetedAttacks.Name: Targeted Attacks and Combinations
targetedAttacks.Hint: Techniques named TA (Skill Attack/Target) and Combination (A + B + C) work out their levels, ceilings and costs; an attack aimed where a TA aims takes its bought levels; Combinations run from the Combat tab; combat techniques also default to Art and Sport skills.

extraEffort.Name: Extra effort in combat
extraEffort.Hint: Giant Step, Great Lunge, Heroic Charge and Rapid Recovery; one offensive and one defensive extra-effort option a turn; Flurry of Blows a point of FP per Rapid Strike attack, halved again; Mighty Blows on Attack only; a critical failure on a new option costs 1 HP.

rangedOptions.Name: Ranged attack options
rangedOptions.Hint: Quick-shooting bows, blowpipes and slings; Rapid Strike and handfuls of thrown weapons; prediction shots that lower Dodge; feints at range; a Heroic Archer's extra aim.

cinematicRangedOptions.Name: Cinematic ranged options
cinematicRangedOptions.Hint: Quick-shooting in combat without the realistic -4, and handfuls of BL/20 lbs. of any small thrown weapon.

unfamiliarWeapons.Name: Unfamiliar weapons
unfamiliarWeapons.Hint: Weapons belong to groups and fighters know some: -2 to wield an unfamiliar weapon, -1 to parry one, and -2 in feints and disarms against one unless both sides face the unfamiliar.

unorthodoxWeapons.Name: Unorthodox weapon use
unorthodoxWeapons.Hint: Two-handed weapons in one hand for the strong, melee weapons hurled, and everyday items improvised as weapons.

shovesAndShields.Name: Shoves, slams and shields
shovesAndShields.Hint: Shoves with weapons and shields, cross-checking slams with long weapons, striking at shields and cloaks, and grabbing them.

untrainedFighters.Name: Untrained fighters
untrainedFighters.Hint: Fear and the Coin Toss for those with no combat skills or Combat Reflexes; Committed and Defensive Attack, Feints, Deceptive Attacks, Rapid Strikes and Defensive Grips need a melee skill at DX level.

harshRealism.Name: Harsh Realism for Unarmed Fighters
harshRealism.Hint: Bare-handed parries against weapons at -3 with the limb in the way, low-line parries, footwork dives, skull blows that hurt, the off hand, and bruised knuckles.

grapplingOptions.Name: Grappling options
grapplingOptions.Hint: All-Out and Committed Attacks in grappling, one-handed strangles, more actions after a grapple, throws from locks, sprawling, and defense while grappling.

longWeaponsInClose.Name: Long weapons in close combat
longWeaponsInClose.Hint: -4 skill a yard of reach, Parry from that skill and -1 swing damage a yard, and a haft attack for long polearms.

grabAndSmash.Name: Grab and Smash, and pain
grabAndSmash.Hint: All-out grapple and strike, Kiss the Wall, locks and strangles that cause pain instead of injury, and -4 to attack from inside a grapple.

bodiesInClose.Name: Teeth and bodies in close combat
bodiesInClose.Hint: Everyone can bite and hold on, with what a bite reaches set by size; extra arms and legs in grappling.

partialInjuries.Name: Partial injuries
partialInjuries.Hint: Wounds to an arm, leg or the torso start to hurt after 2×HT seconds: DX, Dodge and Move penalties by how bad they are.

extremeDismemberment.Name: Extreme dismemberment
extremeDismemberment.Hint: A cut that severs an arm, hand, leg or foot the victim is using may carry through to the other one.

severeBleeding.Name: Severe bleeding
severeBleeding.Hint: Severed parts, the neck, skull, veins and vitals bleed faster and harder; First Aid takes the same penalty, and some need Surgery.

lastingInjuries.Name: Lasting injuries
lastingInjuries.Hint: A major wound to the neck, skull, veins or vitals rolls on its table for a lasting or permanent effect.

whoDrawsFirst.Name: Who draws first
whoDrawsFirst.Hint: A GM tool settles a standoff between two fighters drawing weapons: Fast-Draw, weapon skill, and who strikes first.

chargingFoes.Name: Charging foes
chargingFoes.Hint: Weapon skill against an evader, striking him for half damage on a win; a foe hurt by a stop thrust must force his way past the weapon or run himself onto it.

stopHits.Name: Stop Hits
stopHits.Hint: A Wait may attack into the foe's attack: both roll to hit, and the one who does worse defends at -1, or -3 parrying with his attacking weapon.

cascadingWaits.Name: Cascading Waits
cascadingWaits.Hint: A GM tool rolls the Quick Contest for several Waits triggering together and posts the order they act in.

matterOfInches.Name: A matter of inches
matterOfInches.Hint: Weapon length and weight in who draws first, Stop Hits and Cascading Waits, and weight in feints, Beats, multiple parries and parrying flails.

chambara.Name: Chambara fighting
chambara.Hint: Masters (Trained by a Master or Weapon Master) leap, trade attacks for steps, retreat for +3 again and again, use acrobatics with every defense, and sense attacks from behind; Flying Leap, Light Walk and Lizard Climb gain their chambara feats.

contestOfWills.Name: Contest of Wills
contestOfWills.Hint: A Concentrate challenges a foe to a turn-by-turn contest of Will; the loser reacts with the margin as a bonus, and attacks the winner at that penalty.

concentration.Name: Concentration
concentration.Hint: Giving in to a distracting disadvantage (not Berserk or Bloodlust) leaves a fighter at -2 DX.

fear.Name: Fear and martial artists
fear.Hint: Gruesome wounds offer the GM a Fright Check without the heat-of-battle bonus, and known victories add to Intimidation of minor NPCs.

fakingIt.Name: Faking it
fakingIt.Hint: Stage Combat defaults to Combat Art and Sport at -2 and to combat skills and Performance at -3; a GM tool rolls a faker against a trained fighter.

unarmedEtiquette.Name: Unarmed Etiquette
unarmedEtiquette.Hint: Weapons and shields can't parry or block unarmed attacks.

shakingItOff.Name: Shaking It Off
shakingItOff.Hint: A PC may spend 1 FP right after a failed knockdown roll to stay standing.

shoutItOut.Name: Shout It Out!
shoutItOut.Hint: A secret style lets a fighter shout one attack (-1 to defend) or defense (+1) per style per battle.

proxyFighting.Name: Proxy fighting
proxyFighting.Hint: Techniques through objects and people: -4, the borrowed part's penalty, or an unwilling puppet's ST/2.

bulletTime.Name: Bullet Time
bulletTime.Hint: A GM tool spends 3 unspent points for one turn in stopped time, against defenseless foes.

tournaments.Name: Tournament combat

adjustingForSm.Hint: Gear marked "adjust for SM" weighs, costs and draws power by the size of whoever carries it: half as much for SM -1, twice for SM +1, and on up to x2,000 at SM +10.

legalityAndAntiques.Name: Legality and antiques
legalityAndAntiques.Hint: An obsolete gadget may be carried at a higher Legality Class: one step for every two full tech levels it is behind the campaign, at most two steps and no higher than LC4. Also the price below which a gadget is too simple to need maintenance checks.

powerCells.Name: Power cells
powerCells.Hint: Gear runs on the cells its table line gives. Non-rechargeable cells last twice as long and give twice the shots, a superscience cell gives a weapon five times the shots, and a cosmic cell never runs down. The Gear tab tracks each gadget's endurance and changes its cells in the seconds their size takes. Gadgets can be rigged to smaller cells with Electrician-2, and cells that blow up are explosives with a REF set by TL. Gear with no cell data, the Basic Set's beam weapons among it, is unaffected (their Shots already assume superscience cells).

computers.Name: Computers and software
computers.Hint: A computer's Complexity from its model and TL (+2 at TL10, +1 per TL after), its storage, and the programs it runs at once (two of its own Complexity, ten times as many per level below). Hardware options (compact, fast, genius, hardened, high-capacity, printed, quantum, slow, FTL) reprice it and change its Complexity and LC. A program without a listed price costs what the Software Cost Table gives at the campaign's TL. A program used as a tool gives +1 at Complexity 4 or 5 and +2 at 6 or 7, by the skill's difficulty. Each computer shows the highest-IQ AI it could run, and a GM tool works out how long breaking encryption takes.

swarmbots.Name: Swarmbots
swarmbots.Hint: Build a swarm from its area in square yards, microbots or nanobots, chassis, power supply and type, with a second type for a multi-function swarm, a disguise or self-replication. The item is repriced and shows the swarm's statistics, Move and endurance. A GM can turn it into a swarm NPC that the Basic Set's swarm rules fight. A GM tool runs a second of a combat swarm against its targets: devourers and disassemblers stopped only by sealed DR, stingers and terminators by Sealed (only stingers slowed by clothing), gremlins' damage and malfunction number on machinery, and sentries against other swarms.

robots.Name: Robots
robots.Hint: For a character built from the book's robot templates, the Traits tab shows the body's price with its lenses, and the AI software's price (the Software Cost Table at the Complexity its IQ needs, +5% per extra mental point, never under 20%). It also shows whether the computer the body carries runs that AI (one size smaller for a total cyborg), the robot's LC, and the size of its digital backup. A GM tool reprograms an AI: Electronics Repair (Computers) with physical access, or Computer Programming (AI) against its IQ, at +3 against an Automaton. A critical hit from a surge attack knocks out anything Electrical.

cinematicRobots.Name: Cinematic robot combat
cinematicRobots.Hint: The movie ways of beating robots. A robot knocked back rolls IQ at -2 a yard or is stunned for a turn, even if nothing got through its DR. Automaton robots don't dodge. GM tools cover paint on the sensors (DX or Throwing at -10, then an IQ roll against panic) and a logical paradox (a Quick Contest of Psychology, Fast-Talk or Computer Programming (AI) against a sapient robot's IQ).

stealthSystems.Name: Stealth systems
stealthSystems.Hint: Worn chameleon and invisibility surfaces, cloaks and nets add to Stealth against whatever sense the character says they're hiding from, halved while moving as the book says. Programmable camouflage adds to Camouflage by terrain, scent masking gives +4 to Tracking to cover a trail, and an active flesh mask gives +3 to Disguise. Attacks on a holobelt's wearer are at -1, and on a moving invisible one at -6. The Gear tab lists the detection penalties from infrared cloaking, radar stealth and jammers. Cloaks and nets, shape-memory disguises (half the LC) and tools whose bonus the book states are priced and applied.

securitySystems.Name: Security systems
securitySystems.Hint: A GM tool runs a barrier against the targeted characters. Laser fences can be avoided at Acrobatics-3 or Escape-3 when open and burn when tight. Cutting wire takes DX-5 or cuts. Fragwire bursts, monowire cuts by how fast someone walks into it, and sonic barriers nauseate at HT-6. A neural disruptor field is resisted at HT-1 with sealed armour, a dream net at Will-4 unless Sealed, and a disintegrator field ignores DR. Doors, safes and locks show their DR and modifiers by TL, and scanners carry their bonus to Search.

restraints.Name: Restraints
restraints.Hint: A row action on cufftape, razortape and electronic cuffs breaks free: a Quick Contest of ST against the restraint's ST, or Escape (at -6 or -8 for cuffs). Tape does a point of damage on each failure, and razortape cuts whoever breaks it by force. Cuffs get tougher by TL. A row action resists a power damper (Quick Contest of Will), neuronic restraints (HT-5) and a neural pacifier (the higher of HT-3 and Will-3).

interrogation.Name: Interrogation and lie detection
interrogation.Hint: Sensory restraints worn by the subject add to Interrogation, and a veridicator adds +TL/2 to Detect Lies (and is an automatic success). GM tools run neural programming (a Regular Contest of Brainwashing against Will at -1 per 5 points of the disadvantage, plus the software's quality) and mind probes (Electronics Operation (Medical), slow or fast, where a fast probe risks brain damage or a coma).

uploading.Name: Uploading and downloading minds
uploading.Hint: GM tools upload and download minds. A destructive upload rolls Physician-5 and Electronics Operation (Medical)-5 (Surgery for a bush robot): failing by 1 leaves a low-res copy, by 2 a very-low-res one, by 3 or more nothing. A non-destructive scan takes an hour: low-res only at TL10, full at TL11, or low-res in 10 minutes at +2. A critical failure quietly drops a step. Dead brains are at -2, -1 an hour, and -3 frozen. Downloading rolls Electronics Operation (Medical): a failure destroys the host's brain, and a critical failure or failure by 5+ hides a flaw. A low- or very-low-res copy can be applied to the host (skill points halved or quartered, amnesia, -1 IQ, 50% Flashbacks).

communicators.Name: Communicators
communicators.Hint: A comm's sheet shows its range by size and TL. Receive-only comms are 10% of the cost and 20% of the weight, transmit-only 90% and 80% (half each for gravity-ripple, neutrino and FTL comms). A GM tool checks whether the selected and targeted characters' comms reach each other: the smaller comm's range, times 3, 10, 30 ... for the larger one's sizes. Stretching it takes Electronics Operation (Communications) at -1 per 10%, to double.

sensors.Name: Sensors
sensors.Hint: Worn night vision optics, infrared, hyperspectral and PESA goggles, glasses, contacts and binoculars give Night Vision, Infravision, Hyperspectral Vision and Telescopic Vision (a level per doubling of magnification, growing by TL). Sound detectors add to Hearing and Shadowing, chemsniffers to Tracking and Smell, sensor gloves to touch, and imaging and terahertz radar to Search for concealed weapons. Active sensors show their range, LPI and emissions, and tactical ones are priced. A row action locks a sensor on the target for +3 to aimed ranged attacks, which an ESM detector warns of for +1 to Dodge. A GM tool runs a sweep at -2 per doubling of range past the sensor's.

neuralInterfaces.Name: Interfaces, VR and sensies
neuralInterfaces.Hint: A worn HUD or neural interface gives +1 to Driving, Piloting and Free Fall, and a visual enhancement program +1 to Vision. Row actions experience a sensie (surface mode is -3 to other tasks and +4 to Fright Checks), use a virtual tutor at skill 12, and take a dose of instaskill nano: a point in a skill with a point or less, with an IQ roll against Phantom Voices when doses stack. Items explain VR levels and managers, translators, dreamgames, dream teachers and neural interfaces.

fabrication.Name: Tools and fabrication
fabrication.Hint: A GM tool works out how long an item takes to make, and what it costs, on a production line, fabricator, robofac, nanofac or replicator, with its blueprint's Complexity and its instructor kit. Row actions apply repair nanopaste (1d-2 HP, better with a repair roll), stress a rope past its load (HT 12 at -1 per multiple), and set off an antimatter trap. A GM tool runs slipspray (DX, +3 crawling, -3 sprinting), super adhesives (a Regular Contest of ST against 23) and tractor beams (a Quick Contest of ST against the beam's). Rope, foam, tractor beams and fabricators show their figures by TL.

gravityControl.Name: Gravity control
gravityControl.Hint: A GM tool rolls DX for everyone crossing a gravity gradient: a shift of 10% or more, at -2 per doubling or halving past the first. It notes high acceleration and zero-G nausea. Gravity plates, screens, mats and grav hammers show their figures by TL.

psiAmplifiers.Name: Psi amplifiers
psiAmplifiers.Hint: Row actions attune an amplifier (Electronics Operation (Psychotronics)) and set it to boost a power's Talent by up to its TL limit. Rolls naming that power get the boost. A critical failure, or any roll of 15+ through an amplifier that isn't attuned, burns it out and calls for HT+3 at -boost: a seizure on a failure, a coma on a failure by 5+.

vehicleSystems.Name: Vehicle systems and personal flight
vehicleSystems.Hint: A GM tool deploys crashwebs (ablative DR equal to TL; DX-2 each turn to get free), shares out limited life support, rolls DX+3 for running on a slidewalk, and lands a life pod or drop capsule (Navigation (Space)-12: within a mile, within 5dx100 miles less 200 per point of margin, anywhere, or a disaster). Row actions fire a zero-G thruster's bursts (Free Fall, counting down the cylinder) and strap on flight and thruster packs. The nuclear jetpack's plasma wash and +3 to be spotted, and the capsules' figures, are on their sheets.

matterTransmission.Name: Matter transmission
matterTransmission.Hint: MT booths are priced by range (10 to 10,000 times for continental to interstellar) and teleport projectors by platforms and send-only. An equipped minigate is a shield of DB 4, and a blow its DB stopped (or one blocked with it) goes through the gate. A GM tool rolls a teleport projector (Electronics Operation (Matter Transmitters) at -1 per 1,000 miles, +4 between projectors) and an MT interceptor's Quick Contest.

beamWeapons.Name: Beam weapons
beamWeapons.Hint: The GM sets a scene's air pressure, water and humidity from a tool, and beam weapons follow it. X-ray lasers, grasers, ultraviolet lasers and pulsars reach only so far through air, and rainbow lasers and blasters lose range in vacuum. Lasers barely work underwater, and sonic weapons carry by the pressure. An electrolaser is only its burn in vacuum and is harder to aim in the wet; it stuns, and its kill setting spends two shots and can stop a heart. DR resists an electrolaser or an omni-blaster's stun, a microwave disruptor only reaches the Electrical, and force fields stop graviton beams at a hundredth of their DR and disintegrators at a tenth.

laserOptions.Name: Laser options
laserOptions.Hint: High-energy lasers can be built with dazzle and blinding modes (+10% each) and as pulse or pulse-beam lasers (+100%), and switched between settings on the item. Dazzle is a HT-5 affliction that blinds for minutes equal to the margin; blinding is HT-10 and blinds for good; Protected Vision and a Nictitating Membrane help resist both. A pulse is crushing and explosive, a step less divisor, at twice the range. The attacker can say the beam crosses weather, which adds DR equal to the vision penalty along its path, or strikes glass, which gives a (10) divisor. An eye a laser cripples is crippled for good.

neuralAndSonic.Name: Neural, psionic and sonic beams
neuralAndSonic.Hint: Neural disruptors are built with settings (agony, ecstasy, neural stun, paralysis, seizure, death beam; +50% for each after the first) and switched between them. A failure afflicts for minutes equal to the margin; agony and ecstasy stop a heart on a failure by 5, and a death beam on any failure. They reach nobody sealed, nor machines and bodies without a brain. Mind disruptors are resisted by Will with Mind Shield added: dazing, choking or maddening beams. Mindrippers leave a coma. MAD beams add DR to the roll and inflict agony while in the beam. Sonic stunners add a point per 5 DR and knock out; nauseators pain and sicken anyone who can hear, with Protected Hearing adding 5; screamers take their victims' hearing.

beamOptions.Name: Beam options
beamOptions.Hint: Beam weapons can be field-jacketed or FTL, which frees them from the air and water limits the beam weapons switch applies, and FTL beams have their 1/2D at Max. Lasers, microwave and particle beams can take gravitic focus, up to TL-9 levels: each halves the damage, multiplies the range by 10 and doubles the cost, and can be turned off.

hotshots.Name: Hotshots and overheating
hotshots.Hint: A beam weapon that fires more than ten times its RoF without a 10-second pause between attacks overheats, and malfunctions on 14 until it has cooled for a minute. A hotshot spends two shots for +1 damage per die, or a 30% deeper resistance penalty, at Malf. 14 (12 while overheated). Gatlings don't overheat and can't fire hotshots; neither can plasma guns on cartridges.

firearmAccessories.Name: Firearm accessories
firearmAccessories.Hint: Scopes, rails, harnesses, access control, self-destruct, D-tags, IFF, smartgrips, gravitic compensators and tripods are fields on a weapon that reprice it. Every TL9+ firearm has a laser sight, HUD link, grip or ring and diagnostic computer. On an aimed shot a targeting scope adds +2 to +5 by TL, a point a second aimed; without one, a worn HUD's link adds +1 within 300 yards. Targeting software adds +1 or +2 to its Guns or Gunner specialization. A mounted weapon with that software and a locked tactical sensor gets its Acc instead of every other targeting bonus. Gyrostabilized harnesses and servomounts cancel Move and Attack's Bulk; an articulated harness braces and cuts ST to two-thirds; a smartgrip takes 1 off ST; a compensator makes ST 0 and Recoil 1; a tripod lifts a mounted weapon's ST. Power holsters add TL/2 to Fast-Draw, TacNet +1 or +2 to Tactics, and a sniper mirror lets a laser fire around corners at -4.

warheads.Name: Warheads and ammunition
warheads.Hint: Each ranged mode of a gun, launcher, grenade or mine is loaded with one of the book's warheads its calibre and TL allow, and its row fires it: armour-piercing, hollow-point, memory baton, monochain, shotshell and burrow darts change the round; APHEX, HE and concussion rounds keep it with a follow-up or linked blast; shaped charges, HEMP, SEFOP, thermobaric, stingray, force, plasma and implosion warheads use the book's table by size; EMP, strobe, warbler and psi-bomb warheads are area afflictions with their effects; tanglers, flares, jammers, biochemical fillers, swarms, stasis and vortex warheads are noted for the GM; mininukes and antimatter come in their yields. Proximity-fused HE is an attack at +4.

bladeTech.Name: Ultra-tech blades
bladeTech.Hint: A cutting or impaling weapon can have a superfine (+2, (2), x6 cost), monowire (+2 cutting, (10), x10), hyperdense (+2, (5), weight and ST x1.5) or nanothorn (corrosion, (10), x20) edge, and a vibro field (+1d cutting, +1 at TL11 and +2 at TL12, (3), or (5) superfine and (10) hyperdense; x10, x30 with superfine) switched on with a Ready. The book's exclusions are refused. A rocket striker on an axe, pick or spear adds +6 Striking ST and +3 to the ST needed for a boosted blow, six uses at TL9 doubling per TL. Monowire whips and switchblades take a length within their reach; a switchblade's blade adds its reach to damage and switches to a whip with a Ready; a snare pulled taut cuts thrust+1d(10) each turn. A GM tool pulls off a limpet mine.

energyMelee.Name: Stunners and neurolashes
energyMelee.Hint: Stun wands, zap gloves, neurolashes and neurogloves spend their cell's strikes (a zap glove's kill counts twice). Nonmetallic armour adds +2 per DR to resist a stunner; a failure knocks the victim down paralysed until a HT-5 roll, which a GM tool makes. A neurolash or neuroglove strikes with the neural disruptor's outcome for its setting; from TL11 it can be built with several (+50% each), and only a high-power one delivers a death beam. A neurolash can be added to any melee weapon for $500, and a sonic shuriken can carry a drug sprayer.

forceSwords.Name: Force swords
forceSwords.Hint: Force blades, glaives, swords and whips and the stasis switchblade can't break. A variable force sword (+$500) sets its reach from C to 2. A force blade cuts the weapon it parries or that parries it short of a critical success, only another force blade or a sonic blade unharmed: a row action rolls its damage against the targeted character's weapon.

threatProtection.Name: Threat protection
threatProtection.Hint: Worn suits, helmets and masks give what they protect against as traits: a suit only once the helmet or mask that seals it is on. Sealed, Vacuum Support, Pressure Support, radiation PF, climate control as Temperature Tolerance, glare and hearing protection as Protected Vision and Hearing, a mask's Protected Vision and Smell, and an air supply as Doesn't Breathe, which a carried air tank gives a mask or sealed helmet. The item's sheet shows don times and a tank's hours at its TL, and a row action patches a suit with Vacc Suit rolls.

laserResistantArmor.Name: Laser-resistant armour
laserResistantArmor.Hint: Ablative armour takes its full DR against any laser and loses a point of it at the spot struck for every 10 points of basic laser damage. Reflec and retro-reflective armour take theirs against lasers and microwaves but not X-ray or gamma-ray lasers, and retro-reflective armour bounces half of what it stopped back at the attacker. Transparent bioplas (twice the price) is no use against lasers, and a rigid helmet made reflective (+$50) gets +20 DR against lasers and microwaves. Reflec gives +1 to a radar sweep to find its wearer, +2 for a full suit.

tailoredArmor.Name: Tailored armour
tailoredArmor.Hint: Flexible armour can be tailored: choose the coverage of each part of the body (full, front or back, half, a front or back half, skimpy or none), a style (heavy, normal, light or diaphanous) and a cut (average, stylish or a fashion original). The outfit is priced from the suit, its DR follows the style, a blow to a part it doesn't cover, or from an arc it doesn't face, meets none of it, and half or skimpy coverage takes an activation roll.

armorSystems.Name: Armour systems
armorSystems.Hint: Electromagnetic armour doubles DR, or triples it for laminate, against shaped charges and plasma, counting its uses. Beam-adaptive armour triples DR against the beam types it is set for and adapts to one that hurts it. Reactive paste adds DR against high-velocity attacks and detonates, with fewer chances to cover a spot hit again. Ablative foam gives DR 8 against burning, worn away point for point. Living metal doubles the price. Nasal filter plugs give +5 HT against gas, and biomedical sensors on a patient +1 to Diagnosis.

biochemicalAgents.Name: Biochemical agents
biochemicalAgents.Hint: Riot, nerve, sleep and paralysis gas, pheromone spray, radiant prism, and nerve and sleep poisons (and their contact versions, +2 to resist) are poisons the system doses and cycles: offered in the sheet's Poison dialog, and dosed on targeted characters from the item or a GM tool, rolled at once where there's no delay. A failure does what the agent does: nausea or retching in riot gas, unconsciousness for the margin's minutes in sleep gas, a fall, paralysis or a coma in paralysis gas, drowsiness or sleep from sleep poison. The nerve agents bring coughing, nausea and Neurological Disorder as a third, half and two-thirds of HP go. A sealed suit keeps out contact and breathed agents, no breathing or filter lungs breathed ones, and Immunity to Metabolic Hazards all of them. Musk, smoke, mask, firefoam and metal embrittlement are on their items and the GM tool, with a cloud's duration by the wind.

nanoweapons.Name: Metabolic nanoweapons
nanoweapons.Hint: Nanoburn paralyses for three minutes a point of failure and then does 1d-1 every three minutes for half an hour. Dominator nano rolls after six hours (a minute if superscience) and is priced at $100 a point of the disadvantage, doubled to reverse itself or for superscience. A parasite seed takes 3 HT each failed hour until a success kills it. The GM tool detonates splatter after Aegis has contested it a minute at a time, -1 a die per win and gone after six, and runs shrike against Aegis. Nanoweapons are priced by delivery: blood x2, contact gel x2, contact gas x10, respiratory x5.

propellantSettings.Name: ETC, liquid propellant and velocity
propellantSettings.Hint: A conventional slugthrower can be ETC (1.5 times piercing damage and range, twice the cost, a cell in the grip for 10 magazines) or liquid-propellant (1.5 times the shots a magazine holds and the cost, a bottle for three magazines). Liquid-propellant and electromagnetic guns choose a velocity when firing: boosted is +1 damage a die, low is half damage and -3 to hear it. Air guns can be made non-metallic for 1.5 times the cost.

gyrocsAndLaunchers.Name: Gyrocs, missiles and grenades
gyrocsAndLaunchers.Hint: A gyroc's piercing damage is divided by 3 at one or two yards and by 2 out to 10, unless it fires another warhead. Firing an IML or MLAWS rolls 2d burning backblast for a 2-yard cone behind it, a TML 4d for 3 yards; a reactionless missile has none and five times the Max range. Smart grenades (+$100 at TL9, free after) are programmed with three Readies for a delay, radio command, impact or anti-tamper fuse. A saucer grenade bounces round a corner at -3, a vortex ring at -2 and -10% range a bounce, and a limpet mine is pulled off without its code at ST-5.

homingProjectiles.Name: Homing projectiles
homingProjectiles.Hint: A ranged mode can load infrared (skill 13, x4 cost), multispectral (14, x10; passive, anti-radiation or active) or superscience multiscanner (12, x10) homing rounds, +1 skill per TL after each was introduced, where the round is big enough for its TL. The row becomes a homing attack at the seeker's skill, homing by its sense.

poweredSuits.Name: Powered suits
poweredSuits.Hint: A worn exoskeleton or battlesuit that is switched on and has power left adds its Lifting and Striking ST, Arm ST, Super Jump, Basic Move and Enhanced Move, and carries its own weight (except a lower-body exoskeleton, a power sleeve and an exofield belt). DX rolls and DX-based skills are held to Battlesuit skill while a suit that limits them is powered, -1 more in an unfitted TL9-10 suit. A switchable cybersuit can turn its augmentation off. A lower-body exoskeleton and a gravpack carry a load weightlessly, the gravpack at -1 DX per 40 lbs. until the wearer is used to it. An exofield belt gives no DR without power. Row actions suit up (a Battlesuit roll halves the checkout) and refit a suit.

medicalGear.Name: Medical gear
medicalGear.Hint: Automeds, suitcase docs, pocket medics, suit docs and paramedical swarms treat with their own skills through the system's First Aid, physician's rounds and surgery. Bandage spray and plasti-skin stop bleeding (the spray restores 1 HP); a smart bandage rolls its own First Aid-12 for 1d. A patient attached to life support makes daily mortal wound checks with the unit's bonus (+2 hospital, +1 transport or automed). A medical bed gives +3 to a physician's rounds, medical supplies +1, the best of them counting. Hibernation and neural inhibitors from their items.

ultraTechDrugs.Name: Drugs and nano
ultraTechDrugs.Hint: Morphazine, soothe and crediline are dosed and resisted through the system's poison rules (sleep for 8 hours a point of failure, euphoria for five minutes a point, Gullibility for 25-HT minutes). The other drugs and nano are taken from their items: analgine, antirad, hyperstim (and its wearing off), ascepaline (with its weekly limit), purge, memory-beta, tailored and programmable immune machines (a Physician roll clears illnesses), quickheal (1d, once an hour), critical repair nano, respirocytes (breathing not needed), torpine (24 hours out, then healed at 1 FP) and fast regeneration nano. A drug's form sets its price: aerosol or contact x2, aerosol contact x10. Aegis nanobots keep out metabolic nanoweapons.

regeneration.Name: Regeneration and revival
regeneration.Hint: Nanostasis and revival from it by the supervisor's Physician roll; regeneration tanks healing 1 HP per 12 hours (an hour in a chrysalis machine, twice as long on a failed roll); rejuvenation's outcomes; a chrysalis machine reviving the dead at -2 an hour dead; the pocket regenerator's bandaging and First Aid in a minute; and the regeneration ray healing everything at high power, or 3d toxic and no treatment for 1d weeks on a failure.

forceScreens.Name: Force screens
forceScreens.Hint: A force screen meets a blow before armour with semi-ablative DR (its record), which regenerates a point a second for every 10 DR as world time passes, on or off. While worn and powered it is sealed with pressure and vacuum support and radiation PF equal to its DR. The variants reprice it and change what it stops: energy and kinetic screens stop only their kind of attack, a velocity screen only ranged ones, an adjustable screen reinforces its front or back half, a permeable screen can let air through. A barrier screen's diameter reprices it and sets its SM.

forceShields.Name: Force shields
forceShields.Hint: Force shield bracelets are shields used with Shield (Buckler): DB 3 and DR 100. A reflective force shield's row action rolls DX to return a blocked beam's damage to the attacker. Force wards are noted for the GM.

stasisAndTime.Name: Stasis and time
stasisAndTime.Hint: A stasis belt, cube, chamber or grid, or a tau-shield set to infinity, puts its user in stasis for the time set (row action), and no damage gets through. A worn, powered life support belt gives DR 5 against energy attacks, divides radiation by 10, adds 60°F to the hot side of the comfort zone and seals the wearer unless set to breathe. The tau-shield's sheet shows its time rate and power by level. Reality stabilizers and hypertime fields are noted for the GM.

cybernetics.Name: Cybernetics
cybernetics.Hint: Each implant's trait and equipment record shows its procedure at its TL. A GM tool runs the Surgical Procedures Table for the targeted patient: install, remove or salvage an implant with the Surgery roll (Mechanic (Robotics) for salvage), the time, the injury on a failure, the recovery (halved on a critical success, doubled without robotic instruments), the fee, and the critical failures. The implant's trait is out of play until its recovery ends, and electrical implants go out of play after an EMP or microwave surge. Another GM tool finds implants. Second-hand and salvaged parts, chip slots, cognitive enhancement, weapon mounts, uplift and neurotherapy or psych implants are priced by their fields, and a psych implant's removal rolls Will against its lasting.

Gadget.Title: Ultra-Tech
Gadget.RuggedHint: Built to withstand abuse: +2 HT, twice the DR, a fifth more weight and twice the price (Ultra-Tech p. 15).
Gadget.DisguiseHint: Built into something else of a similar shape: twice the price mass-produced, five times custom-built (Ultra-Tech p. 15).
Gadget.StylingHint: Made as fashionable as possible: 2 to 10 times the price, by how elaborate it is and the reaction bonus it brings (Ultra-Tech p. 15). Zero for a gadget with no styling.
Gadget.GradeHint: Cheap: half the price, half again the weight. Expensive: twice the price, two thirds the weight. Power cells are left out of the weight either way (Ultra-Tech p. 15).
Gadget.CellWeightHint: What the cells in the gadget weigh, which cheap and expensive leave out of their weight (Ultra-Tech p. 15).
Gadget.BuildHint: What the gadget is built from, for the DR the book assumes: plastic DR 2, a weapon DR 4, a solid metal melee weapon DR 6, and armour or a vehicle its own (Ultra-Tech p. 17).
Gadget.HealthHint: The HT the gadget's own entry gives; zero to assume HT 10 (Ultra-Tech p. 17).
Gadget.AdjustForSmHint: The note the tables print after a gadget's weight, cost and power: all three go by the size of whoever carries it (Ultra-Tech p. 16).
Gadget.PricedAt: Built: ${cost} and {weight} lbs. (x{factor} the listed price).
Gadget.Sized: Adjusted for SM {sm}: weight, cost and power cells x{factor}.
Gadget.Antique: Obsolete at TL{campaign}: carried as LC{lc} rather than LC{was}.
Gadget.Maintained: Worth maintenance checks at TL{campaign}: it costs more than ${threshold}.
Gadget.Simple: Too simple to maintain at TL{campaign}: under ${threshold}, assume it works indefinitely.

Power.Title: Power
Power.SupplyPack: a {size} cell, worn as a pack
Power.FlexibleHint: Flat cells stuck on like stamps: AA and A cost the usual, larger ones four times as much (Ultra-Tech p. 19).
Power.NonRechargeableHint: Last twice as long, or give twice the shots, but can't be recharged (Ultra-Tech p. 19).
Power.CosmicHint: Unlimited power to an ordinary device, at a hundred times the price; LC2, or LC1 for E and F cells (Ultra-Tech pp. 19-20).
Power.SuperscienceHint: Five times the weapon's shots (Ultra-Tech p. 133). The Basic Set's beam weapons already assume these cells; divide their Shots by 5 for mundane ones.
Power.TlHint: The TL the cells were made at, where it isn't the gadget's; zero for the gadget's own. Sets how hard an exploding cell hits (Ultra-Tech p. 19).
Power.ShotsUnlimited: No count of shots: a cosmic cell never runs down.
Power.Blast: If the cells explode: {dice}d cr ex (REF {ref} at TL{tl}).
Power.BlastHint: At the GM's option, cells may explode when destroyed, as an explosive of their weight with a REF by TL (Ultra-Tech pp. 19-20; damage by Campaigns p. 415).
Power.RigHint: Ten cells one size smaller stand in for one larger cell. Rigging it is Electrician-2 and ten minutes a try, and a critical failure damages the gadget (Ultra-Tech p. 19).
Power.RigDone: Rigged to run on {cells} {smaller} cells in place of its {size}, after {minutes} minutes' work.
Power.RigFailed: The rig didn't take: another {minutes} minutes to try again.
Power.RigDamaged: The rig went badly wrong: the gadget is damaged.
Power.UsedHint: Hours the gadget has run on these cells. Cells keep their charge indefinitely when not in use (Ultra-Tech p. 18).
Power.WeaponHint: A weapon's cells are changed with its Reload button, which offers Fast-Draw (Ammo) to take a second off (Ultra-Tech p. 19).

Computer.Title: Computer
Computer.KindHint: A computer is one of the book's standard models; a program is rated by its Complexity (Ultra-Tech pp. 22, 24).
Computer.ModelHint: The standard model: its Complexity and storage at TL9, and +2 Complexity at TL10, +1 per TL after (Ultra-Tech p. 22).
Computer.ExtraStorageHint: Storage built in on top, at $1 and 0.001 lb. per unit: terabytes at TL9, petabytes at TL10, and so on (Ultra-Tech p. 23).

Option.compactHint: Twice the cost, half the weight; half the cells and half the operating time.
Option.fastHint: +1 Complexity at 20 times the cost. Not with Slow or Genius.
Option.geniusHint: +2 Complexity at 500 times the cost; LC -1. Not with Fast or Slow.
Option.hardenedHint: +3 HT against EMP, microwaves and other attacks on electrical gadgets; twice the cost and weight.
Option.highCapacityHint: Runs half again as many programs at once, at 1.5 times the cost.
Option.printedHint: Printed on fabric or skin, four square feet per pound; -1 Complexity and a thousandth the storage. Runs on solar or flexible cells. Not quantum.
Option.quantumHint: 10 times the cost, twice the weight, LC -1; +5 Complexity to break encryption.
Option.slowHint: -1 Complexity and a tenth the storage, at a twentieth the cost. Not with Fast or Genius.
Option.ftlHint: Superscience (TL11^): +1 Complexity at 100 times the cost, twice the weight; LC -1.

Computer.Figures: Complexity {complexity}, {storage} {unit}. Runs {own} programs of Complexity {complexity} at once, or {below} one level below.
Computer.CompactCells: Compact: half the power cells and half the operating time.
Computer.Hardened: Hardened: +{bonus} HT against attacks on electrical gadgets.
Computer.ComplexityHint: The least Complexity a computer must have to run the program (Ultra-Tech p. 21).
Computer.DifficultyHint: The difficulty of the skill a software tool is for: an Easy skill needs less Complexity for the same bonus (Ultra-Tech p. 25).
Computer.RunsOnHint: Which of the character's computers the program is running on.
Computer.MassMarketHint: Software sold to a huge user base costs as little as a tenth of the table's price (Ultra-Tech p. 24).
Computer.TablePrice: ${cost}: Complexity {complexity} at TL{tl} on the Software Cost Table.
Computer.Unavailable: Complexity {complexity} software is unavailable at TL{tl}.

Tool.basic: Too simple to give a bonus to {skills}: good needs Complexity {good}, fine {fine}.
Tool.good: A good tool for {skills} (+1); fine needs Complexity {fine}.

Computer.TooComplex: Too complex for this computer to run.
Computer.OverloadedHint: More programs than the computer runs at once: two of its own Complexity, ten times as many per level below.

Encryption.Title: Break encryption
Encryption.NoRoller: Select a token to roll its Cryptography.
Encryption.Result: {standard} encryption at TL{tl} needs Complexity {needed} for an hourly attempt. Complexity {complexity}{quantum}: each attempt takes {time}.

Swarm.Title: Swarm
Swarm.SquareYardsHint: The swarm's area. Its price is per square yard; a square yard weighs about two pounds (Ultra-Tech pp. 35, 37).
Swarm.BotsHint: Microbots are insect-sized (TL10) and nanobots cell-sized (TL11); nanobots can ooze through cracks (Ultra-Tech p. 35).
Swarm.ChassisHint: The bots' bodies and how they move, which change the price (Ultra-Tech p. 36).
Swarm.PowerHint: What runs the bots, and what it adds to the price (Ultra-Tech pp. 36-37).
Swarm.TypeHint: What the swarm does, from the Swarm Type Table (Ultra-Tech p. 37).
Swarm.SecondTypeHint: A multi-function swarm, microbots at TL11 or nanobots at TL12, combines two types at their added cost, doing one at a time (Ultra-Tech p. 37).
Swarm.ExtraModelsHint: A repair swarm costs $250 more per square yard for each further kind of equipment it repairs (Ultra-Tech p. 37).

Hints.underwaterInfrared: An infrared laser can't get through more than a few inches of water: range 0/1 (Ultra-Tech p. 114).
Hints.underwaterBlueGreen: A blue-green laser's range underwater is 150 yards in crystal-clear water, 60 in average water and 15 in murky water (Ultra-Tech p. 115).
Hints.ultravioletAir: In atmosphere, an ultraviolet laser's range can't exceed 500 yards divided by the air pressure (Ultra-Tech p. 115).
Hints.noRangeUnderwater: This beam has no range underwater (Ultra-Tech pp. 115-125).
Hints.rainbowVacuum: In vacuum or trace air a rainbow laser defocuses: range divided by 10, and no armor divisor (Ultra-Tech p. 116).
Hints.rainbowWater: A rainbow laser has an underwater range of two yards (Ultra-Tech p. 116).
Hints.xrayAir: X-rays are absorbed by air: range 7/20 yards in a standard atmosphere, divided by the air pressure, unless field-jacketed (Ultra-Tech p. 117).
Hints.graserAir: Gamma rays are absorbed by air: range 70/200 yards in a standard atmosphere, divided by the air pressure, unless field-jacketed (Ultra-Tech p. 118).

Hints.pulsarAir: In atmosphere an antiparticle beam's range can't exceed 1,000 yards divided by the air pressure, unless field-jacketed (Ultra-Tech p. 124).
Hints.electrolaserVacuum: With no air to ionize, an electrolaser only inflicts its laser's burn (Ultra-Tech p. 119).
Hints.electrolaserHumid: The bolt jumps off the laser path in moist air: -2 to hit (Ultra-Tech p. 119).
Hints.electrolaserRain: The bolt jumps off the laser path in rain, drizzle or heavy fog: -6 to hit (Ultra-Tech p. 119).
Hints.sonicVacuum: Sonic weapons don't work in vacuum or trace air unless touching the target (Ultra-Tech p. 124).
Hints.sonicPressure: Sonic range is multiplied by the air pressure, to at most twice the listed range (Ultra-Tech p. 124).
